title: Move Zeroes — two-pointer compaction.
shortTitle: Move Zeroes — Two-Pointer Compaction Keeping Order

s1_definition.profdef: Move Zeroes rearranges an array so that all zero values move to the end while the relative order of the non-zero values is preserved, done in place. It uses a same-direction two-pointer compaction: a slow pointer marks where the next non-zero value goes, and a fast pointer scans every element, placing each non-zero at the slow position. After the scan, the remaining tail is filled with zeros. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya has a list of this month's charges where cancelled charges show as zero. She wants all the real charges pushed to the front in the same order they happened, with the zeros swept to the back. She keeps one finger on the next clean slot and scans with another; every real charge gets written forward, then the leftover slots at the end become zeros.
s1_definition.oneliner: Write every non-zero to the front with a slow pointer, then pad the rest with zeros — order preserved, no extra array.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Move Zeroes rearranges an array so that all zero values move to the end while the relative order of the non-zero values is preserved, done in place. It uses a same-direction two-pointer compaction: a slow pointer marks where the next non-zero value goes, and a fast pointer scans every element, placing each non-zero at the slow position. After the scan, the remaining tail is filled with zeros. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya has a list of this month's charges where cancelled charges show as zero. She wants all the real charges pushed to the front in the same order they happened, with the zeros swept to the back. She keeps one finger on the next clean slot and scans with another; every real charge gets written forward, then the leftover slots at the end become zeros.

**One line to remember:** Write every non-zero to the front with a slow pointer, then pad the rest with zeros — order preserved, no extra array.

sections.s2_technical:
The clean approach has two phases but a single pass does most of the work. Phase one: a slow pointer `insert` starts at 0, and a fast pointer `i` scans the whole array. Whenever `a[i] != 0`, you write `a[insert] = a[i]` and advance `insert`. After this phase the first `insert` slots hold all non-zero values in their original order. Phase two: fill indexes from `insert` to the end with 0.

A code snippet: `void moveZeroes(int[] a) { int insert = 0; for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { if (a[i] != 0) { a[insert++] = a[i]; } } while (insert < a.length) { a[insert++] = 0; } }`. The relative order of non-zeros is preserved because we copy them in the order we encounter them.

An alternative single-phase swap version avoids the fill loop: whenever `a[i] != 0`, swap `a[i]` with `a[insert]` and advance `insert`. This keeps zeros and non-zeros moving in one go and writes fewer times when zeros are rare. Both are O(n); the swap version minimizes writes, which can matter on write-expensive media.

A senior nuance is "stability," meaning the non-zero order must not change, which the copy and swap approaches both guarantee because they move elements left only into already-processed slots. A common mistake is sorting or using a partition that reverses order; that fails the ordering requirement. Also note the problem says in place, so allocating a second array is a disqualifying answer even though it is trivially correct.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India shows Priya's monthly statement, but cancelled line items appear as zero amounts scattered through the list. The UI wants all real charges grouped at the top in the exact order they occurred, with the empty placeholders at the bottom. This is exactly how Move Zeroes works — non-zeros are compacted forward preserving order, zeros pushed to the tail.

Problem 2 — The statement array is large and shared, so we must not allocate a copy; we rearrange the same array in place.

The code shows a `StatementCompactor` with `moveZeroes`, a demo on Priya's charge array with scattered zeros, and the compacted output.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: charges [15000, 0, 32000, 0, 0, 5000, 48000].

Step 1: The slow pointer `insert` is 0. The fast pointer `i` is 0 with value 15000, which is non-zero, so it is written to slot 0 (no change) and `insert` becomes 1.

Step 2: `i` is 1 with value 0, skipped. `i` is 2 with 32000, written to slot 1 and `insert` becomes 2. `i` is 3 and 4 are zeros, skipped.

Step 3: `i` is 5 with 5000, written to slot 2 and `insert` becomes 3. `i` is 6 with 48000, written to slot 3 and `insert` becomes 4. The scan ends with the first four slots holding 15000, 32000, 5000, 48000 in original order.

Step 4: The fill loop runs from index 4 to 6, writing zeros. The final array is 15000, 32000, 5000, 48000, 0, 0, 0.

Step 5: Order of the real charges is exactly as they first appeared, and all cancelled zeros are at the end, all without a second array.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Before: [15000, 0, 32000, 0, 0, 5000, 48000]
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    After : [15000, 32000, 5000, 48000, 0, 0, 0]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Move Zeroes rearranges an array so every zero ends up at the back while the non-zero values keep their original order, and it must be done in place. I treat it as a same-direction two-pointer compaction. A slow pointer marks the next slot for a non-zero value, and a fast pointer scans the whole array; each time the fast pointer sees a non-zero, I copy it to the slow slot and advance the slow pointer. After that single pass, the front holds all the non-zeros in order, and I fill the remaining tail with zeros.

The property interviewers test is stability, meaning the non-zero order must not change. The copy approach preserves it naturally because I write non-zeros in the exact order I meet them, only ever moving them left into slots I have already processed. If I instead sorted or used an order-breaking partition, I would get the zeros in place but fail the ordering requirement. There is also a swap variant that moves zeros and non-zeros in a single phase and minimizes the number of writes when zeros are rare, which is worth mentioning.

The in-place constraint is the whole point of the problem. Allocating a second array and filtering is trivially correct but disqualifying, so I always stay within the original array using only two index variables.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the statement service. Priya's monthly statement had cancelled line items showing as zero amounts scattered through the list, and the UI wanted the real charges grouped at the top in the exact order they occurred with the empty placeholders at the bottom. I compacted the shared statement array in place to avoid copying a large structure. Explaining the slow-and-fast compaction, the stability guarantee, the swap alternative, and the in-place constraint shows the interviewer I know both the algorithm and why each rule exists.
